title: Winter and Well
premise: Hospice nurse Marguerite Iversen has spent her life documenting the backwards-counting of the dying, believing that writing things down keeps them contained. When her childhood imaginary friend, Wren, appears on her porch unchanged after thirty years, Marguerite learns she was chosen as a child to be a 'keeper'—someone who memorizes a harvest song whose final verse must never be sung aloud before the moon rises full. As patients begin dying in the wrong order and her estranged sister arrives demanding answers, Marguerite must choose between loyalty to Wren, who saved her once, and the truth that Wren is the thing the song was written to hold back. In the end, Marguerite sings the last verse alone under the rising moon, unmaking Wren—and discovering that the friend was the part of herself she buried to survive, now finally grieved and released.
about_author: Astrid Amberdale is the pen name of a former night-shift caregiver who writes folk horror from a farmhouse in rural Minnesota. Her work explores the quiet terrors of duty, memory, and the stories we tell ourselves to keep the dark at bay.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. On a night shift at Rosewood Hospice, patient Alma counts backwards from ninety without drawing breath, and Marguerite documents it in her leather journal as she always does. The beat is ritualistic calm masking dread—we see her coping mechanism of documentation as prayer, and learn she has filled eleven journals since childhood.

chapters.title: Porch Light
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Arriving home at dawn, she finds a small figure waiting on her porch: Wren, her childhood imaginary friend, unchanged at seven years old while she is nearly forty. Wren says only, 'You stopped writing about me.' The beat is uncanny recognition—the past refusing to stay documented and dead.

chapters.title: Eleven Journals
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, with journal excerpts. She rereads her childhood journals and finds pages about Wren torn out—pages she doesn't remember removing. Each torn page leaves a scar of missing memory: a summer, a well behind the house, a song. The beat is mounting self-distrust; her archive, her religion, has been edited by her own hand.

chapters.title: Alma's Last Verse
chapters.summary: Alma's POV, brief and fragmentary. Dying Alma hears the song too—a harvest tune her own grandmother forbade her to finish. She grabs Marguerite's wrist and hums three notes before counting backwards one last time. The beat is inherited fear, revealing the song spans generations of women who were all 'keepers.'

chapters.title: Sister of Record
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Her estranged sister Delphine arrives unannounced, having received an anonymous letter claiming Marguerite is 'singing again.' Their reunion crackles with old wounds—Delphine remembers nothing of Wren and insists their childhood was ordinary. The beat is gaslit friction between loyalty and denial.

chapters.title: What Wren Wants
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, childlike and wrong. Wren explains they waited because the song is almost complete: Marguerite learned all but the last verse as a girl, and the harvest moon is coming. Wren only wants to 'hear it finished,' framing it as love. The beat is tender menace—affection weaponized.

chapters.title: The Well Behind the House
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She visits her demolished childhood home and finds the old well still open in the new owners' overgrown lot. At its lip she hears humming from below, in her own voice. The beat is physical horror and the first hard evidence that Wren is not imagination but something housed in the ground.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She begins a twelfth journal solely for Wren, testing whether writing contains or feeds the thing. Entries she writes appear altered by morning—her handwriting, kinder words. The beat is the collapse of her core belief: some truths cannot be archived into safety.

chapters.title: Patients Out of Order
chapters.summary: Multiple staff POVs braided. Hospice patients begin dying ahead of schedule, each found counting backwards, each humming the same three notes. Administrator Priya questions Marguerite's late-night presence. The beat is professional unraveling—Marguerite's secret bleeding into the ward she swore to protect.

chapters.title: Delphine Remembers Water
chapters.summary: Delphine's POV. Triggered by the anonymous letter's phrase 'the well,' Delphine dreams of drowning and wakes with mud on her feet. She confronts Marguerite, who admits Wren has returned. The beat is reluctant alliance—two sisters choosing shared truth over comfortable lies.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Burden
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, researching. In the county historical society she finds a 1911 ledger of 'harvest keepers'—women listed by generation, each entry ending mid-sentence except the first, which names the song 'Winter and Well' and warns: 'the last verse is a door.' The beat is dread through genealogy; she is the latest link in a chain.

chapters.title: Three Notes More
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren teaches Marguerite the fourth verse in dreams, sweetly, patiently, insisting the song wants to be whole. Marguerite wakes each morning with the melody closer to complete and her reflection slightly delayed. The beat is seduction—horror as grooming, love as erosion of identity.

chapters.title: Priya's Suspension
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. After a patient dies clutching Marguerite's twelfth journal page, Priya suspends her pending investigation. Marguerite loses the ward, her routine, her prayer. The beat is exile—stripped of duty, she has nothing left between herself and the song.

chapters.title: What the Torn Pages Said
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Using water damage and indentations, she recovers fragments of the torn childhood pages: 'Wren fell in. Wren is in the well. I sang so it would sleep.' She realizes she didn't invent Wren—she made a bargain as a child, trading memory for her sister's life. The beat is devastating reframe: the imaginary friend was a rescue she paid for in forgetting.

chapters.title: Loyalty
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren reminds Marguerite of the bargain's terms: finish the song and Wren goes free; refuse and the debt collects someone else—Delphine. Wren genuinely believes it loves her. The beat is moral vertigo—loyalty to a savior who is also a captor, love against duty made literal.

chapters.title: The Anonymous Letter
chapters.summary: Delphine's POV. Delphine traces the letter to their grandmother's house, long sealed, and finds drafts in the grandmother's hand—written decades ago, addressed to whichever granddaughter became keeper next. The beat is chilling inheritance: the letter wasn't a warning from an ally but instructions from a dead woman's trap.

chapters.title: Verse Against Verse
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Cross-referencing the 1911 ledger with her recovered pages, she deciphers the truth: the last verse isn't a key that frees Wren—it's a lock that unmakes whatever wears Wren's shape. Every keeper before her sang it alone or died incomplete. The beat is clarity won at cost; knowledge arrives too late to be safe.

chapters.title: Harvest Moon Rising
chapters.summary: Braided POV, short sections. The moon rises fat and orange. Patients across the county sit up in bed, counting. Wren stands in Marguerite's kitchen, singing verses one through four, waiting for her to join on the fifth. Delphine pounds on the locked door. The beat is converging siege—everything arrives at once.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Alone with Wren, hearing Delphine scream outside, Marguerite makes her choice: she sings the fifth verse solo, voice cracking, refusing harmony, refusing the duet Wren needs. The well-thing tears at the seams of its borrowed shape. The beat is climax—love expressed as refusal, duty fulfilled as betrayal.

chapters.title: Unmaking
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, dissolving. As the verse completes, Wren experiences something like gratitude—the shape was always a cage for it too. It asks Marguerite, in her own childhood voice, to remember it kindly. Then it is gone, and the porch is empty, and the counting stops everywhere at once. The beat is grief and release entangled.

chapters.title: After the Moon
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Days later: patients rest quietly, Priya lifts the suspension, and Delphine stays to help pack up the journals. Marguerite writes a final entry—not containment this time, but eulogy—for Wren, for the girl who bargained, for the version of herself that stayed invisible. The beat is mourning transformed into witness.

chapters.title: Twelfth Journal, Last Page
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, closing frame. She visits the filled-in well, now capped with concrete and wildflowers, and reads the last verse aloud one final time—not as a lock, but as a lullaby. Somewhere far off, faintly, a child laughs, and does not count. The beat is bittersweet resolution: identity reclaimed, truth survived, love outlasting the thing that wore its face.
